muscles.name: Adductor longus and brevis (with gracilis, pectineus)

volume_training_variables.recommended: Start each mesocycle near MEV (~8-12 hard sets/muscle/week) and progress upward
volume_training_variables.description: MASS/Helms recommend, absent personal historical data, starting at ~8-12 hard sets per muscle per week (the published dose-response starting zone) and then progressing load/reps before adding sets. RP frames this as MEV, the mesocycle starting volume, which then ramps toward MRV. This is the entry point for volume-based progressive overload, not the ceiling.

volume_training_variables.recommended: 10-20 hard sets/muscle/week; growth keeps rising with diminishing returns
volume_training_variables.description: Schoenfeld/Ogborn/Krieger 2017 meta found a graded dose-response with hypertrophy increasing through 10+ weekly sets/muscle (favorable over ~9 sets), but had insufficient data above that. Pelland 2026 meta-regression (67 studies, 2058 participants) confirms a positive volume-hypertrophy slope (100% posterior probability slope>0) with diminishing returns: roughly a 3:2 scaling (tripling volume ~doubles growth, e.g. ~3% growth at 6 sets vs ~6% at 18 sets). Baz-Valle 2022 review converges on 12-20 weekly sets/muscle as the optimum standard recommendation. Caution past ~25 fractional sets where data thin out.

volume_training_variables.recommended: 12-20 weekly sets/muscle (trained, training each muscle 2x/week)
volume_training_variables.description: Baz-Valle 2022 meta-analysis of RCTs in young trained men (>=1 yr experience) found NO significant difference between moderate (12-20 sets) and high (>20 sets) weekly volume for quadriceps (p=0.19) or biceps brachii (p=0.59) hypertrophy, with trivial effect sizes (-0.2 and -0.1). Thus 12-20 weekly sets is the optimum standard recommendation for trained young men, with no consistent extra benefit from exceeding 20. Increasing frequency may allow more volume to be tolerated.

volume_training_variables.recommended: 20-30 weekly sets/muscle as a high-volume starting point if maximizing growth
volume_training_variables.description: Stronger By Science, interpreting the Pelland meta-regression, recommends 20-30 weekly sets/muscle as a starting point for lifters whose goal is to MAXIMIZE (not merely efficiently approach) hypertrophy, divided across the chosen frequency (e.g. 25 sets = 5x5, 4x6, 3x8, or 2x12). Above ~25 fractional weekly sets the data are sparse, so the true plateau/junk-volume point is unknown; the authors caution it could lie anywhere from ~25 to 50-60+ sets. Most time-constrained trainees will land under 15 sets/muscle and still grow well.

volume_training_variables.recommended: 30-40 weekly sets only for short specialization on 1-2 priority muscles
volume_training_variables.description: Weightology (Krieger) notes that 21+ weekly sets is realistically achievable only via specialization, focusing very high volume (30-40 weekly sets, counting direct + indirect) on 1-2 muscles while keeping others at maintenance, rotating priority every 2-4 months. Studies driving the upper end (e.g. Radaelli 6-month, 30-45 arm sets) used young subjects; older/less-recovered lifters may not tolerate it. This is an upper bound for emphasis blocks, not a standing recommendation.

volume_training_variables.recommended: ~6-10 weekly sets/muscle drives near-maximal early growth in novices
volume_training_variables.description: For novices, minimum effective volume sits close to maintenance volume because growth comes easily; RP places MEV near ~6 sets early on, and meta-analytic dose-response (Schoenfeld 2017) shows clear benefits emerging around 9-10+ weekly sets. Lower weekly volumes that fail trained lifters still grow beginners well, so ~6-10 sets/muscle is a sufficient, efficient novice starting range, scaled up over time as MEV rises.

volume_training_variables.recommended: Medium (5-9) to high (>=10) weekly sets/exercise beat low (<=5) for strength
volume_training_variables.description: Ralston 2017 meta-analysis (9 studies, 223 males) found a graded weekly-set dose-response for strength: medium (MWS, 5-9 sets/exercise/week) and high (HWS, >=10) produced greater 1RM gains than low (LWS, <=5). Combined effect: HWS vs LWS ES 0.18 (95% CI 0.06-0.30, p=0.003); MWS vs LWS ES 0.15 (p=0.04). Differences are trivial-to-small in magnitude but consistent, and held for both multi-joint and isolation exercises.

volume_training_variables.recommended: >=5 sets/exercise/week (medium volume); avoid single low-set programs
volume_training_variables.description: Ralston 2017 concludes that for novice and intermediate male trainees, low weekly sets (<=5/exercise) do NOT produce strength gains comparable to medium (5-9) or high (>=10) weekly sets, for both multi-joint and isolation lifts. So beginners targeting strength should perform at least medium weekly volume per exercise rather than minimalist single-set work.

volume_training_variables.recommended: Either medium (5-9) or high (>=10) weekly sets/exercise is appropriate for trained lifters
volume_training_variables.description: Ralston 2017 reports that for well-trained males the sparse data indicate either MWS (5-9) or HWS (>=10) weekly sets/exercise is an appropriate dose for strength, with HWS marginally favored but no clear separation from MWS. This is closer to an EQUIVALENCE between medium and high weekly volume for strength in the trained, unlike the clearer low-vs-medium gap seen in novices.

volume_training_variables.recommended: More weekly volume aids strength but with steep diminishing returns; modest volumes capture most of it
volume_training_variables.description: Pelland 2026 meta-regression found the volume-strength slope exceeds zero with 100% posterior probability, but the diminishing returns for strength are CONSIDERABLY MORE PRONOUNCED than for hypertrophy. Strength is largely a skill/neural adaptation, so lower-moderate weekly volumes capture most of the strength benefit and extra sets add little; high volume is far more justified for size than for maximal strength.

volume_training_variables.recommended: ~6-8 quality sets/muscle/session before per-session returns flatten (long rests)
volume_training_variables.description: Weightology's convergence-of-evidence synthesis (protein synthesis, anabolic signaling, satellite cell, and meta-analytic data) clusters around 'more volume is better up to ~6-8 sets per training session' per muscle when using long (2+ min) rests; with shorter rests the per-session need may be higher. This is the per-session stimulus ceiling that motivates spreading high weekly volume across multiple sessions rather than cramming it into one.

volume_training_variables.recommended: Late-workout sets done with reduced effort (half-assed) become junk volume
volume_training_variables.description: Stronger By Science clarifies that 'junk volume' is ill-defined but is most real when per-set EFFORT drops late in long sessions: extra sets taken far from failure (e.g. lackadaisical lunges/extensions after hard squats and presses) likely contribute little. Additional sets are not inherently junk; with maintained 0-2 RIR effort they still add value. The practical junk-volume risk is effort decay, not set count per se.

volume_training_variables.recommended: ~11 fractional sets/session is the per-session strength ceiling (point of undetectable superiority)
volume_training_variables.description: The Remmert per-session volume meta-regression (cited in Pelland and SBS) reports a 'point of undetectable outcome superiority' (PUOS) of ~11 fractional sets per workout for strength - beyond that you should be <50% confident more per-session volume adds strength. Marginal value per set is already halved by ~set 5. This per-session ceiling interacts with frequency: more than 11 sets may help when a muscle is trained only 1x/week but is excessive at high frequencies.

volume_training_variables.recommended: MV ~6 sets/muscle/week to maintain existing mass (e.g. during deloads/deficits)
volume_training_variables.description: Renaissance Periodization Maintenance Volume (MV) landmark: roughly 6 working sets per muscle per week (trained >=2x/week) preserves existing muscle mass, for novices and advanced alike. Used during deloads, fat-loss phases, busy periods, or when deprioritizing a muscle to focus volume elsewhere. Below MV, muscle is lost; MV is the floor of the landmark system (MV < MEV < MAV < MRV).

volume_training_variables.recommended: MEV ~8-12 sets/muscle/week as the mesocycle starting volume
volume_training_variables.description: Renaissance Periodization Minimum Effective Volume (MEV) is the lowest weekly volume that actually grows muscle and serves as the START of each mesocycle. For intermediates it sits well above maintenance (RP's worked example uses a 12-set MEV); the gap between MV and MEV widens with training experience. Identified per-muscle via pump/challenge/soreness self-assessment, then progressed upward through MAV.

volume_training_variables.recommended: MAV: ramp from MEV toward MRV across a mesocycle (e.g. 12->20 sets, +1-3/week)
volume_training_variables.description: Renaissance Periodization Maximum Adaptive Volume (MAV) is the progression ZONE between MEV and MRV where best gains occur - not a fixed number. RP's worked mesocycle ramps 12 (MEV) -> 14 -> 16 -> 18 -> 20 (approaching MRV) -> deload, adding 1-3 sets/week guided by recovery and performance feedback. Volume must climb within a block because tolerance rises with accumulated training. This 12-20 zone aligns with Baz-Valle's meta-analytic 12-20 optimum.

volume_training_variables.recommended: MRV ~20+ sets/muscle/week - upper recoverable limit; back off when performance drops
volume_training_variables.description: Renaissance Periodization Maximum Recoverable Volume (MRV) is the per-muscle upper limit beyond which recovery fails and gains stall; in RP's example MRV is ~20 sets. Signs you've hit it: you can't match the prior week's performance despite adequate rest. Briefly touching MRV can trigger supercompensation, but chronically training at/above it kills progress - respond with a recovery session, deload to MV, or start a new mesocycle at MEV. MRV is highly individual and exercise-dependent (fatiguing compounds lower it).

volume_training_variables.recommended: At matched weekly volume, frequency has negligible effect on hypertrophy - count total weekly sets, distribute as you like
volume_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE finding: Pelland 2026 meta-regression found the frequency-hypertrophy slope was compatible with NEGLIGIBLE effects (posterior probability of slope>0 was <100%) once weekly volume is equated. So for size, total weekly set volume is the driver and frequency is mainly a tool to fit that volume under the per-session ceiling. (For STRENGTH, by contrast, the same meta found frequency does help, slope>0 at 100% posterior, with diminishing returns.) Higher frequency mainly matters because it lets you accumulate more weekly volume below the per-session junk threshold.

volume_training_variables.recommended: ~5-10 sets/muscle/week is the most time-EFFICIENT range (captures ~half of maximal growth)
volume_training_variables.description: Stronger By Science, using the Pelland ~3:2 volume:growth scaling, shows efficiency and maximal results are opposing goals: ~5-10 weekly sets captures roughly half the growth of ~30 sets in a third of the gym time. Marginal value per set is already halved by ~set 5 and it takes ~3 added sets at 15/week to match the value of your first weekly set. So 5-10 sets is the recommendation when training efficiency (not absolute maximum) is the priority - relevant for time-constrained trainees.

volume_training_variables.recommended: 9 sets grows biceps; ~18 sets (moderate) showed the largest growth response
volume_training_variables.description: Schoenfeld et al. 2019 (IJSPP) RCT randomized 49 trained men to 9, 18, or 27 weekly biceps sets for 6 weeks. Muscle thickness rose significantly in ALL groups (4.3%, 9.5%, 5.4% for LOW/MOD/HIGH) with no statistically significant between-group difference, though effect sizes were moderate-to-large favoring MOD/HIGH over LOW. Demonstrates 9 sets in one session suffices to grow a muscle in trained men, while ~18 sets produced the numerically largest response.

volume_training_variables.recommended: >20 total weekly sets favors triceps growth (synergist in pressing)
volume_training_variables.description: Baz-Valle 2022 found the triceps brachii is the one muscle showing a clear volume dose-response: high volume (>20 total weekly sets) significantly beat moderate volume (p=0.01, ES -0.5 favoring high). Because triceps act as synergists (not prime movers) in many multi-joint presses, more total sets are needed to accumulate equivalent direct stimulus; ~12-20 sets of DIRECT triceps work may be optimum once indirect pressing volume is counted.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2x/week per muscle (minimum), distribute weekly sets over >=2 sessions
loading_training_variables.description: Foundational hypertrophy frequency recommendation from Schoenfeld 2016 frequency meta-analysis: on a volume-equated basis, training each muscle 2x/week produced superior hypertrophy to 1x/week (binary frequency effect ES 0.49 +/- 0.08 high-freq vs 0.30 +/- 0.07 low-freq, p=0.002), so major muscle groups should be trained at least twice weekly. Whether 3x beats 2x at matched volume remained undetermined (insufficient sample). This is a partial-equivalence finding: once volume is held constant, the 1x-vs-2x gap is real but going beyond 2-3x adds little independent benefit.

loading_training_variables.recommended: Any frequency 1-6x/week gives similar growth once weekly sets are equated; frequency is a logistics lever, not an independent driver
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE finding: Pelland et al. 2026 dose-response meta-regression (67 studies, 2058 participants) found the posterior probability of the frequency-on-hypertrophy slope exceeding zero was LESS than 100%, i.e. compatible with negligible effects once weekly volume is accounted for. Contrast with volume, whose slope was 100% positive. Practical reading: distribute your target weekly set count across however many sessions fit your schedule/recovery; per-muscle frequency at matched volume is roughly equivalent for size.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-4x/week per muscle as the practical sweet spot; pick the frequency that lets you accumulate target weekly volume with quality sets
loading_training_variables.description: Synthesis of the matched-volume hypertrophy literature: Schoenfeld 2016 establishes >=2x as the floor; Currier 2023 Bayesian NMA ranked higher-load multiset TWICE-weekly as the single highest-ranked prescription for hypertrophy, while noting all prescriptions promoted comparable hypertrophy. SBS analysis of 13 volume-matched studies found each extra training day added only ~0.11%/week of growth (small, d~0.11 overall). 2-4x lets most lifters hit modern volume targets (~10-20 sets/muscle/wk) without crushing per-session volume.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-3x/week per muscle; untrained lifters show the largest frequency benefit
loading_training_variables.description: In SBS's matched-volume hypertrophy analysis, untrained subjects in higher-frequency groups grew ~47% faster than lower-frequency groups (0.58 vs 0.39%/week, d=0.62, p=0.0014) — a larger relative advantage than trained lifters (~32%). The frequency benefit is most pronounced when per-session volume is low and recovery is fast, both typical of novices. Full-body or upper/lower splits hitting each muscle 2-3x/week are well supported for beginners.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-4x/week; in trained lifters frequency matters mainly as a way to fit higher weekly volume
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE-leaning finding for trained lifters. SBS's trained-subject subgroup (9 studies) found higher frequency grew ~32% faster at matched volume (0.58 vs 0.44%/week, d=0.38, p=0.016) — smaller than untrained. Schoenfeld et al. 2019 (N=49 trained men) found 18-27 biceps sets over 2 sessions vs 9 sets in 1 session produced no significant between-group difference in muscle thickness; the real lever was volume, which higher frequency enabled. Use higher frequency to make a larger weekly volume tolerable rather than as an end in itself.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 3-6 training sessions/week overall to spread per-muscle volume across the body
loading_training_variables.description: Total weekly session count (whole-body frequency) is largely a scheduling consequence of per-muscle frequency and split choice. Hitting each muscle 2x/week typically requires 3-6 sessions depending on the split (full-body 3x, upper/lower 4x, push/pull/legs run 2x = 6x). The hypertrophy literature shows no independent whole-body session-frequency effect once per-muscle volume and frequency are controlled; Schoenfeld 2016 noted matched per-muscle-group session-frequency comparisons couldn't even be analyzed due to inadequate samples.

loading_training_variables.recommended: Use frequency as the lever to raise tolerable weekly volume; distribute current volume first, then add
loading_training_variables.description: Practical distribution principle drawn from the matched-volume metas: because volume (not frequency) is the dominant hypertrophy driver (Pelland 2026 volume slope 100% positive vs frequency compatible with zero), the main value of higher frequency is enabling more weekly volume at acceptable per-session fatigue. Recommended implementation: when increasing frequency, first spread existing weekly sets over more days, hold volume constant until recovery is confirmed, then progressively add volume. Splitting e.g. 20 squat sets into 5 sets x 4 days is tolerable where 20 sets in one session is not.

loading_training_variables.recommended: Raise frequency most when per-muscle weekly volume is low (<10 sets); benefit shrinks at high volume
loading_training_variables.description: Frequency benefit is volume-dependent. In SBS's hypertrophy analysis, low-volume studies (<10 sets/muscle/wk or <60 total sets/wk) showed higher frequency growing ~77% faster (0.57 vs 0.32%/week, d=0.82, p=0.0046, a large effect), whereas high-volume studies showed only ~27% faster (0.58 vs 0.46%/week, d=0.34, p=0.017). Practical rule: add frequency primarily to make low weekly volume more effective or to enable raising volume; at already-high volume, extra frequency yields diminishing hypertrophy returns.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 3-6x/week per lift for advanced/elite strength athletes, used to distribute high volume
loading_training_variables.description: Direct evidence in well-trained lifters is sparse and lower-grade. The Norwegian Frequency Project (conference abstract, never peer-reviewed) reported well-trained powerlifters gained more strength training each lift 6x/week vs 3x/week at equated volume. SBS's direct-comparison analysis showed strength overperformance rising with frequency up to 4-5x/week, but the authors caution they wouldn't extrapolate past ~4-5x and all studies were <=12 weeks. Elite lifters commonly use high frequency to spread large competition-lift volume across the week; treat as expert/practitioner-grade guidance, not settled meta-analytic fact.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 1-3x/week for squat-type lower-body lifts; frequency does NOT clearly help lower-body strength at matched volume
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE finding specific to lower body. Grgic 2018 found no significant frequency effect on lower-body strength at matched volume (p=0.070). SBS's matched-volume analysis: each added day raised lower-body (squat/leg-press/hack-squat) strength by only 0.10%/week (~5% faster, NS, p=0.33); 3+x vs 1-2x was a small, non-significant difference (d=0.35, p=0.27). Likely because lower-body compounds are more fatiguing/slower to recover. Squatters can train 1-3x/week per the lift without sacrificing strength at fixed volume.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-4x/week for multi-joint lifts; frequency benefit on strength is real for compounds but not isolation
loading_training_variables.description: Grgic 2018 subgroup: frequency significantly affected strength tested on MULTI-JOINT exercises (p<0.001) but NOT single-joint exercises (p=0.324). Multi-joint lifts carry a larger motor-skill/practice component, which higher frequency improves (more practice opportunities, higher average bar speed/quality per set). Spreading compound-lift volume over 2-4 days is supported; isolation-lift strength is relatively frequency-insensitive (an equivalence for single-joint movements).

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-4x/week per lift; young/untrained lifters respond positively to higher frequency
loading_training_variables.description: Grgic 2018 found a significant frequency-on-strength effect among young adults (p=0.024) but not middle-aged/older adults (p=0.093). SBS matched-volume analysis: untrained subjects gained strength ~23% faster at higher frequency (3.07 vs 2.50%/week, d=0.43, p=0.02). Novices benefit from frequent skill practice and recover quickly, so 2-4x/lift accelerates strength even at fixed volume.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-5x/week per lift; trained lifters still gain ~20% faster at higher frequency, mainly via added volume tolerance
loading_training_variables.description: SBS matched-volume analysis: trained subjects (8 studies) gained strength ~20% faster at higher frequency (1.78 vs 1.49%/week, d=0.42, p=0.046) — a small but significant effect on par with untrained. Grgic 2018 noted most evidence is in untrained populations and called for more trained-lifter data. Caveat: the 'trained' subjects in these studies were beginner-to-intermediate, so generalization to elite lifters is uncertain. Higher frequency primarily lets trained lifters absorb more weekly volume.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-4x/week per lift; strength keeps rising with frequency but with strong diminishing returns
loading_training_variables.description: Unlike hypertrophy, Pelland et al. 2026 found the frequency-on-strength slope had a 100% posterior probability of exceeding zero — strength gains DO consistently increase with frequency — but with pronounced diminishing returns. This contrasts with the Grgic matched-volume null and reflects that frequency aids strength partly through skill/practice and average set quality, not only added volume. Sweet spot for most lifters is 2-4x/lift; gains past that are small.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-4x/week per lift; the matched-volume frequency-strength effect was significant in women but not men
loading_training_variables.description: Grgic 2018 sex subgroup: frequency significantly affected strength gains in women (p=0.030) but not men (p=0.190). Combined with the upper-body and multi-joint findings, this suggests frequency helps most where there is more headroom for skill/quality improvement. Women training for strength can favor 2-4x/lift; for men the matched-volume frequency effect is closer to an equivalence.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 1-3x/week for middle-aged/older adults; frequency does not significantly change strength gains in this group
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE finding for older populations. Grgic 2018 found no significant frequency effect on strength among middle-aged/older adults (p=0.093), in contrast to young adults (p=0.024). Slower recovery likely blunts any frequency advantage. For older trainees, even 1-2x/week per lift drives strength effectively at matched volume, so frequency can be chosen for adherence/joint tolerance.

loading_training_variables.recommended: Higher-load, multiset, thrice-weekly was the top-ranked prescription for strength
loading_training_variables.description: Currier et al. 2023 Bayesian network meta-analysis (strength network: 178 studies, n=5097) ranked higher-load (>80% 1RM) multiset THRICE-weekly training as the single highest-ranked RTx for strength (SMD 1.60, 95% CrI 1.38-1.82 vs no-exercise control); threshold analysis showed this was extremely robust. Note this couples frequency with load and set number — the standout was the combination, and many prescriptions produced similar calculated effects. Supports ~2-3x/week as a strong default whole-program strength frequency.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 3-5x/week for upper-body pressing (bench/press) — the clearest matched-volume frequency benefit
loading_training_variables.description: The strongest matched-volume frequency signal in the literature is for upper-body pressing strength. Grgic 2018 found a significant frequency effect for upper-body (p=0.004) but not lower-body (p=0.070) strength. SBS's matched-volume strength analysis found each added training day raised upper-body strength gains by 0.51%/week (~28% faster, p=0.019), and 3+x vs 1-2x produced a large effect (d=0.93, p=0.0056); removing outliers raised d to 1.18. Spreading pressing volume over 3-5 days clearly helps strength even at fixed volume.

loading_training_variables.recommended: Volume drives strength; at matched volume, frequency per lift is roughly equivalent (use frequency to add volume)
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE finding from Grgic et al. 2018 strength frequency meta (22 studies). Unadjusted, effect sizes rose with frequency (0.74, 0.82, 0.93, 1.08 for 1/2/3/4+x per week, overall p=0.003). BUT the volume-equated subgroup showed NO significant frequency effect (p=0.421). Conclusion: higher frequency improves strength chiefly because it permits more weekly volume; frequency per se has little independent effect once volume is matched. Practical takeaway: greater frequencies are a tool for adding RT volume, which then drives strength.

loading_training_variables.recommended: <60%1RM (commonly 40-60%1RM tested) for relative/absolute muscular endurance
loading_training_variables.description: Light loads (<60%1RM, typically tested at 40-60%1RM) are the conventional endurance prescription. Schoenfeld rep-continuum concludes any load-induced endurance effect, if real, is limited to the far-light end and is more relevant to lower-body and absolute (vs relative) endurance; multiple studies using pre-test 1RM for the endurance test refute a low-load benefit. Low confidence / equivalence-leaning evidence.

loading_training_variables.recommended: very heavy loads (≥80%1RM, 1-6RM) grow muscle but are inefficient/risky for hypertrophy
loading_training_variables.description: Heavy loads CAN build muscle but at a cost. Rep-continuum: heavy-load protocols need more sets to match moderate-load hypertrophy (inefficient), and the powerlifting-style 7×3RM group showed overtraining and joint issues vs a 3×10RM group at equal volume load. Thus for hypertrophy, ≥80%1RM is recommended only as a minor portion of training; moderate loads achieve equal growth more sustainably and time-efficiently. EQUIVALENCE in outcome, divergence in cost.

loading_training_variables.recommended: high loads may slightly favor type II growth but the effect is non-significant
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE (with a non-significant lean toward heavy): Grgic & Schoenfeld fiber-type meta found type II fiber CSA gains favored high-load but not significantly (SMD 0.30, 95%CI -0.05 to 0.66, p=0.089, I²=0%); excluding the one female-subject study (Schuenke) dropped it to SMD 0.20 (p=0.310). So while heavier loads (>60%1RM) might marginally favor type II hypertrophy, current biopsy data do not establish a real difference when training to failure.

loading_training_variables.recommended: load does not reliably bias type I vs type II fiber growth when sets go to failure
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE at the fiber level: Grgic & Schoenfeld fiber-type meta (10 study groups, biopsy) found NO significant load effect on type I fiber CSA (SMD 0.28, 95%CI -0.27 to 0.82, p=0.316, I²=18%). The hypothesized 'light loads preferentially grow type I' claim is not supported by failure-matched data, though confidence/prediction intervals are wide (need more research). Per Henneman's size principle, low loads taken to failure eventually recruit high-threshold units too.

loading_training_variables.recommended: ~30-85%1RM remains load-independent in trained lifters when taken to failure; moderate loads most sustainable
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE holds in resistance-trained individuals. Rep-continuum cites Schoenfeld (~10RM vs ~30RM) and Morton (8-12RM vs 20-25RM) both showing equal muscle-thickness / fiber-CSA / lean-mass gains in trained men. Heavy-load (e.g. 7×3RM vs 3×10RM, volume-load matched) gave equal biceps growth but the heavy group showed overtraining/joint issues — so for trained lifters moderate loads are preferred for sustainability, not magnitude. Trained subjects need MORE sessions/volume to keep growing (Lopez: number-of-sessions interaction p=0.031-0.045).

loading_training_variables.recommended: any load ~30-85%1RM to failure grows muscle; novices respond strongly regardless of load
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE, strongest in novices: Lopez NMA meta-regression found untrained participants exhibit GREATER hypertrophy than trained at the same dose (training-status interaction p=0.033, large window for adaptation) and showed no load-dependence for size when sets go to failure. Mitchell/Lim: 30% and 80%1RM to failure produced ~equal quadriceps volume (6.8% vs 7.2%) and fiber CSA (15-20%) in untrained men. So load choice for novice hypertrophy is essentially free above the ~30%1RM floor.

loading_training_variables.recommended: ≥~30%1RM minimum effective load; below ~20%1RM growth is roughly halved
loading_training_variables.description: There IS a lower load threshold for hypertrophy despite broad load-independence. Schoenfeld rep-continuum: load-independent growth holds for loads ≥~30%1RM. Lasevicius (cited in continuum & SBS): 40/60/80%1RM produced equal CSA gains but 20%1RM produced roughly HALF the growth at matched volume load. Practical floor sits in the 30-40%1RM band; meaningful tension below that is insufficient.

loading_training_variables.recommended: ~30-85%1RM all grow similarly when taken to/near failure; moderate (~60-80%) most efficient
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE result: at matched effort (to/near failure), whole-muscle hypertrophy is essentially LOAD-INDEPENDENT across ~30-85%1RM. Lopez NMA found no difference between low/moderate/high loads for hypertrophy (high vs low SMD 0.12, 95%CI -0.06 to 0.29; I²=0%; all p=0.113-0.469). Schoenfeld rep-continuum/low-vs-high meta: pooled ES 0.03 (95%CI -0.16 to 0.22) — 'there is no ideal hypertrophy zone.' Moderate loads recommended on practical grounds (less discomfort, less time, less joint stress), not greater hypertrophy.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 80-100%1RM (≈1-6 reps) for the lifts you want to get stronger at
loading_training_variables.description: Maximal-strength (1RM) gains are load-DEPENDENT: heavier loads win. Lopez network meta (28 studies, 747 adults, all to failure) found high-load (≥80%1RM / ≤8RM) superior to low-load (>15RM) for 1RM strength (SMD 0.60, 95%CI 0.38-0.82, p<0.001; 98.2% probability of being best). Schoenfeld rep-continuum meta likewise reported ES 0.58 favoring >60% vs ≤60%1RM. Currier Bayesian NMA: the top-ranked prescriptions for strength were all characterized by higher loads (≥80%1RM). Effect is driven by specificity (training resembles the 1RM test) and is largely independent of volume.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 85-100%1RM emphasis; specificity rises with training age
loading_training_variables.description: In trained/advanced lifters the load dose-response for 1RM is MORE pronounced and increasingly specificity-bound: the rep-continuum review states continued max-strength gains become increasingly dependent on training near one's 1RM as the genetic ceiling is approached, and the principle of specificity strengthens with training experience. Helms DUP RCT in resistance-trained men used 65-80%1RM across a 4-8 rep undulating block and both %1RM- and RPE-based loading drove 1RM gains, with RPE giving a small strength edge. Caution: Lopez NMA explicitly excluded highly strength-trained athletes, so elite extrapolation is uncertain.

loading_training_variables.recommended: ≥85%1RM, periodic maximal (≥90%) singles/triples — note: low direct evidence
loading_training_variables.description: For elite strength athletes the evidence base is thin: the rep-continuum review states research in highly trained individuals is lacking and that maximal-strength progress likely becomes increasingly dependent on training close to 1RM near the genetic ceiling. Lopez NMA had NO highly strength-trained subjects (avg relative strength below elite thresholds), so its high-load>low-load result cannot be extrapolated to elites — flagged as a recommendation by mechanism/expert reasoning rather than direct elite data.

loading_training_variables.recommended: ~70-90%1RM (≈5-12 reps); heavy load still wins but novices gain strength on almost any load
loading_training_variables.description: In novices, high load remains superior for 1RM strength but the gap is smaller because untrained individuals improve strength even with light loads. Lopez NMA: high-load > low-load for strength overall (SMD 0.60), and the low-vs-high strength advantage was actually LARGER in older studies / men; untrained subjects still gained with low loads. Rep continuum: significant 1RM gains seen even at ≥20 reps in untrained, just less than heavy. Practical novice strength loading ~70-90%1RM, moderate reps, because skill acquisition dominates early.

loading_training_variables.recommended: moderate (60-79%1RM / 9-15RM) beats low load for strength but trails high load
loading_training_variables.description: Dose-response across the load spectrum for 1RM: Lopez NMA found moderate-load (60-79%1RM, 9-15RM) superior to low-load (>15RM) for strength (SMD 0.34, 95%CI 0.05-0.62, p=0.003), while high-vs-moderate favored high but was non-significant (SMD 0.26, 95%CI -0.02 to 0.54, p=0.068). Practical takeaway: a moderate 9-15RM range still develops strength well and is the recommended fallback for those who cannot tolerate very heavy loads, eliciting both size and strength.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 15+ reps (<60%1RM) for local muscular endurance — evidence is weak/equivocal
loading_training_variables.description: The rightward 'endurance zone' (15+ reps, <60%1RM) is the WEAKEST-supported part of the continuum. Schoenfeld rep-continuum: evidence for a load-specific local-endurance effect is equivocal — early work hinted light loads help absolute endurance (esp. lower body) but findings flip depending on whether pre- vs post-intervention 1RM sets the test load, and heavy-vs-moderate comparisons show no dose-response. Included for completeness of the load/rep continuum; treat as low-confidence.

loading_training_variables.recommended: ~6-20 reps/set (most work in a personal 6-15 'sweet spot'), to within ~0-3 reps of failure
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE: rep range per se has little effect on hypertrophy when sets are taken near failure. SBS (Nuckols) pooled analysis: only ~7% of growth variance explained by rep range (r²=0.074); low/moderate/high reps grew muscle within ~10-15% of each other. Practical hypertrophy range ~6-20 reps; the '6-15 sweet spot' exists because it maximizes hard sets per session/week, not because of a magic zone. Schoenfeld continuum: similar growth across a wide spectrum. Bottom edge matters — see the ~30%1RM minimum-threshold row.

loading_training_variables.recommended: ~60-70% of sets in personal sweet spot, ~15-20% heavier/lower-rep, ~15-20% lighter/higher-rep
loading_training_variables.description: Practical programming heuristic: because different rep ranges trigger growth via partly different signaling pathways, SBS (Nuckols) recommends spanning the spectrum rather than one fixed range — e.g. of 15 weekly sets, ~9-10 in your personal 6-15 sweet spot, ~2-3 heavy low-rep sets, ~2-3 light high-rep sets. This is an EQUIVALENCE-derived recommendation (no single range is magic) optimizing total hard sets and pathway variety, not a claimed superiority of any one range.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 1-6 reps/set (heavy 'strength zone')
loading_training_variables.description: Strength-zone rep range corresponding to ~80-100%1RM. Schoenfeld rep-continuum review affirms a genuine 'strength zone' for 1RM: multiple studies show greater 1RM gains training at 1-5 vs 8-12 reps, and the dose-response is more pronounced in trained individuals. SBS notes low/moderate reps still build some strength but heavy low-rep work yields better 1RM. Lower bound 1, practical working bound ~6 (≈85%1RM); sets of 3-8 are common for compound lifts (SBS).

loading_training_variables.recommended: 1-6 reps emphasis for trained strength athletes (specificity-driven)
loading_training_variables.description: For trained lifters the strength-zone (1-6 reps / ~85-100%1RM) advantage is stronger than in novices: rep-continuum notes the load dose-response for 1RM is more pronounced in resistance-trained individuals and specificity grows with experience, so regular heavy low-rep practice becomes increasingly important for maximizing 1RM. Some sets of 3-8 on main lifts remain practical (SBS). Hypertrophy work in higher ranges still supports the foundation.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 30-90 s short rests to build local muscular endurance / fatigue resistance
loading_training_variables.description: For local muscular endurance, short rests (~30-90 s) are conventionally prescribed to train fatigue resistance and metabolic tolerance, pairing with the high-rep light-load (>=15 reps, <60% 1RM) end of the continuum. Note the evidence for a load/rest-specific endurance effect is weak/equivocal per Schoenfeld et al. 2021 (especially for relative endurance and upper body), so this prescription is expert convention more than strong meta-analytic support.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 1.5-3 min; novices tolerate shorter rests with less volume-load loss, but >=2 min is still the safer default
loading_training_variables.description: The rest-interval hypertrophy literature is dominated by trained subjects; in untrained/novice lifters the penalty of short rest is smaller because absolute loads are low and fatigue accumulates less. Krieger's meta-regression had essentially no long-rest data points <6 sets/session in untrained subjects, so per-session conclusions are extrapolated. General guidance still favors ~2 min so that subsequent sets retain enough reps to be 'hard' (near-failure) sets, which is what drives the volume-hypertrophy dose response.

loading_training_variables.recommended: if using short rests (<2 min), do ~2x the per-session sets to match long-rest gains
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE-WITH-A-COST: short rest is not inferior per se, but it incurs a per-session VOLUME PENALTY. Krieger's volume meta-regression split studies by rest length: with long rests (>=2 min) hypertrophy peaked at ~6-8 sets/muscle/session (breakpoint model, gradual regression after); with short rests (<2 min) hypertrophy kept rising to ~15-16 sets/session. Conclusion: 'with short rest intervals, you have to do approximately twice as many sets per session as with long rest intervals to maximize gains.' So short rest can match long rest only if you roughly double per-session volume to offset the volume-load each short-rested set loses.

loading_training_variables.recommended: when every set is taken to failure, rest length matters little for hypertrophy
loading_training_variables.description: EQUIVALENCE: SBS (Nuckols team) notes that when sets are taken to true failure, hypertrophy is comparable across a wide range of rest intervals (citing Henselmans & Schoenfeld 2014 review plus Ahtiainen 2005 and Buresh 2009, which found no rest-interval difference). The practical reconciliation: rest matters because short rest cuts reps on subsequent sets BELOW failure/near-failure; if you simply do each set to failure regardless of how truncated it is, total effective stimulus tends to equalize - but at the cost of more, lower-quality sets. Hence the >=2 min recommendation is about training efficiency (preserving hard reps per set), not an absolute hypertrophy requirement.

loading_training_variables.recommended: >=2 min to avoid blunting the acute anabolic (MPS) response
loading_training_variables.description: Mechanistic support for longer rest: McKendry et al. 2016 found short (1 min) inter-set rest BLUNTED resistance-exercise-induced myofibrillar protein synthesis and intracellular anabolic signalling versus 5 min in young men. This is the acute counterpart to Schoenfeld 2016's longitudinal finding that 3 min > 1 min for hypertrophy. Acute MPS does not perfectly predict chronic growth, so this is supporting mechanistic evidence, not the primary basis - but it converges with the RCT data toward a >=2 min recommendation.

loading_training_variables.recommended: diminishing returns past ~3 min for hypertrophy; ~2-3 min captures most of the benefit
loading_training_variables.description: The hypertrophy benefit of longer rest is driven by recovering enough to keep reps/load high on subsequent sets; once ~2-3 min restores most of that capacity, additional rest mainly costs session time without proportional hypertrophy gain. Schoenfeld 2016's superior arm used 3 min, and no compelling hypertrophy advantage is established for resting substantially beyond 3 min. For time efficiency, ~2-3 min is the practical sweet spot for hypertrophy (vs the 3-5 min needed for maximal strength).

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-3 min; short rests (<1 min) carry a measurable hypertrophy penalty in trained lifters
loading_training_variables.description: In resistance-TRAINED men, longer rest is where the strongest direct evidence sits: Schoenfeld et al. 2016 randomized trained men to 1 min vs 3 min rest (volume/load otherwise matched in prescription); the 3 min group gained more muscle thickness AND strength. Krieger/Schoenfeld note short rest intervals show a 'potential hypertrophic detriment' in resistance-trained individuals, plausibly confounding studies that used 1 min rest for one arm (e.g. Mangine 2015). Recommend >=2 min for trained lifters chasing hypertrophy.

loading_training_variables.recommended: at least 2 min (120 s) between sets; ~2-3 min is a safe default for compound multi-joint work
loading_training_variables.description: Rest intervals of >=~2 min are superior or equal to short rests for hypertrophy. Schoenfeld et al. 2016 (JSCR) found 3 min rest produced GREATER muscle thickness gains than 1 min rest in resistance-trained men over 8 weeks, attributed to the higher total volume-load preserved with longer rest. Mechanistic data (McKendry 2016) show 1 min inter-set rest blunts myofibrillar protein synthesis vs 5 min. Practical floor is ~2 min; little added benefit demonstrated beyond ~3 min for hypertrophy.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-4 min for large compound lifts (squat, deadlift, press, row) to preserve volume-load
loading_training_variables.description: Large compound lifts deplete more reps with short rest, so for hypertrophy they warrant >=2 min and often 3-4 min to keep each set near failure. Schoenfeld 2016's 3 min > 1 min hypertrophy result used compound movements (e.g. squat, bench). The mechanism is volume-load preservation: short rest reduces reps performed on subsequent sets, lowering the effective hard-set count that drives growth.

loading_training_variables.recommended: ~1-2 min for small single-joint movements (curls, lateral raises, extensions)
loading_training_variables.description: Rest needs scale with the systemic and local fatigue of the exercise. For small isolation movements, recovery between sets is faster and shorter rests (~60-120 s) generally preserve enough volume-load to keep sets near failure. This is a practical refinement of the global >=2 min rule: the 2-3 min floor matters most for large compound lifts where short rest meaningfully cuts reps on the next set.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 3-6 min (sometimes more) for top sets of competition lifts near 1RM
loading_training_variables.description: Elite/advanced strength athletes lifting at very high intensities on the competition lifts often need 3-6 min (occasionally longer) for top singles/doubles to fully recover neuromuscularly and maintain bar speed. This is the upper end of the strength rest prescription; the heavier the absolute load relative to recovery capacity, the longer the rest required to express maximal force.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 3-5 min on heavy compound work; do not shortchange rest at high intensities
loading_training_variables.description: Trained lifters generating high absolute loads need long rest to express strength. Schoenfeld et al. 2016 found 3 min > 1 min for STRENGTH (not just hypertrophy) in trained men, supporting a >=3 min floor for heavy work. As intensity climbs toward 1RM and reps drop, the 3-5 min range is the standard expert recommendation to maintain bar speed and load across sets.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 3-5 min between heavy sets for maximal strength
loading_training_variables.description: For maximal strength (1RM), the conventional and well-supported prescription is 3-5 min rest, allowing near-complete recovery of the phosphagen system and neuromuscular readiness so each heavy, low-rep set can be performed at full intensity. This pairs with the strength side of the repetition continuum (heavy loads, low reps), which Schoenfeld et al. 2021 affirm is supported for 1RM gains via specificity. Longer rest preserves load and reps, which is exactly what strength practice requires.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 3-5 min for main lifts; can use ~2 min for accessory strength work
loading_training_variables.description: Intermediates building strength should rest 3-5 min on primary compound lifts to maintain load and reps across sets, with somewhat shorter rests acceptable on lighter accessory work where the strength stimulus is secondary. This follows the strength specificity principle: practicing heavy lifts at full intensity requires near-full inter-set recovery.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 0-2 RIR with high reps (light load); proximity to failure drives the endurance/metabolic stimulus
loading_training_variables.description: For local muscular endurance with light loads, training close to failure (0-2 RIR) is the relevant stimulus because the high-rep, high-fatigue exposure is the point, and Pelland's RCT found local muscular endurance gains were similar whether the single set was to failure or 2-RIR. With very low loads, getting near failure also matters more for any concurrent hypertrophy (motor-unit recruitment is delayed at light loads), as noted in Grgic/Refalo discussion (Lasevicius: failure favored hypertrophy at 30% but not 80% 1RM). Mechanistic/limited direct evidence: most proximity RCTs target strength/hypertrophy, not endurance specifically.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 0-3 RIR (most sets 1-2 RIR); proximity matters but going all the way to 0 is not required
loading_training_variables.description: For hypertrophy the dose-response is meaningful: muscle growth increases as sets are terminated closer to failure. In Robinson et al. 2024's best-fit meta-regressions the marginal RIR slope was negative with a CI that excluded the null (unlike strength). The Refalo-curve magnitude (per Henselmans' read of it) is ~0.45 SMD at 0 RIR, ~0.30 at 2 RIR, and ~0.20 at 5-8 RIR, i.e. a steep early drop then a long flat tail. Practically, train most sets at 0-3 RIR; the marginal benefit of the last 1-2 reps before true failure is small while fatigue cost rises, so 0 RIR every set is not required. NOTE: Refalo 2023 concluded there is no evidence failure is SUPERIOR to non-failure for hypertrophy, so this is a soft optimum, not a mandate.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 2-4 RIR (RPE 6-8) on main movements to limit muscle damage; chase failure on isolation work instead
loading_training_variables.description: Helms et al. 2016 recommend keeping main movements (squat, bench) primarily in the RPE 6-8 range, i.e. 2-4 RIR, to avoid excessive muscle damage and the resulting intensity decrements on subsequent sets, even when training for hypertrophy. Because the compound lift's fatigue-per-stimulus cost is high, the small hypertrophy premium of going to 0 RIR (Robinson 2024 slope) is better captured on single-joint exercises where systemic fatigue is lower. This is a fatigue-management / stimulus-to-fatigue-ratio recommendation, not a claim that closer-to-failure produces less hypertrophy.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 0-2 RIR on isolation work; taking the last sets to/near failure is low-cost and captures the hypertrophy premium
loading_training_variables.description: On single-joint exercises (curls, extensions, raises) the systemic and neuromuscular fatigue cost of going close to failure is low, so this is where to spend the closer-to-failure hypertrophy premium implied by the negative RIR slope in Robinson et al. 2024. Refalo's fatigue RCT showed acute velocity loss and perceptual cost scale with proximity, but on isolation lifts that cost is small and recovers within 24-48 h. Pelland's single-set RCT (FAIL vs 2-RIR) found several hypertrophy measures modestly favored FAIL with low absolute differences. Practically: 0-2 RIR, with the final set of an exercise often taken to failure.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 0-2 RIR (slightly closer to failure than for novices)
loading_training_variables.description: Evidence hints that more advanced trainees may need a higher intensity of effort to keep growing. Grgic et al. 2022's subgroup for resistance-trained individuals found a small but SIGNIFICANT hypertrophy benefit of training to failure (ES = 0.15, 95% CI 0.03-0.26, p = 0.039), unlike the overall null. Pelland's trained-subject single-set RCT also showed several hypertrophy measures trend toward FAIL over 2-RIR. So for trained lifters, biasing toward 0-2 RIR (rather than 3-4) is reasonable, accepting the higher fatigue cost. Caveat: based on only 2 trained-subject studies in Grgic, so confidence is low.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 1-4 RIR (effort sufficient; precise failure unnecessary and RIR estimates are less accurate)
loading_training_variables.description: Novices grow well across a broad RIR range and need not train to failure: Grgic et al. 2022's overall null (and the Refalo meta) drew mainly on untrained/young samples and found no failure superiority for hypertrophy. RIR estimation accuracy is also poorer in untrained lifters (they tend to call '5 reps to failure' what is actually closer to failure), so a nominal 1-4 RIR target tends to land effectively close enough. Henselmans notes the evidence for needing failure is, if anything, WEAKER in trained vs untrained partly because untrained lifters auto-correct toward failure. Prioritize learning technique and accumulating volume over chasing 0 RIR.

loading_training_variables.recommended: Budget for steeply rising fatigue below ~3 RIR; failure roughly triples acute neuromuscular fatigue vs 3 RIR
loading_training_variables.description: Quantifies the 'big fatigue cost at 0' claim. In Refalo et al.'s crossover RCT (6 sets bench at 75% 1RM in trained men/women), acute post-set lifting-velocity loss scaled LINEARLY with proximity: FAIL -25%, 1-RIR -13%, 3-RIR -8% (failure ~3x the fatigue of 3-RIR). Within-session first-to-last-set velocity loss was -22% (FAIL) vs -9% (1-RIR) vs -6% (3-RIR). At 24 h, FAIL and 1-RIR still showed ~-3% decrement vs +2% for 3-RIR; by 48 h all recovered. Perceived discomfort, exertion, and soreness all worsened nearing failure. So the marginal fatigue/soreness cost of the last few reps is large and outlasts a day, while the hypertrophy premium is small.

loading_training_variables.recommended: Hold ~3-6 RIR during deload weeks to shed accumulated proximity-driven fatigue
loading_training_variables.description: Because acute neuromuscular fatigue and soreness rise linearly with proximity to failure (Refalo fatigue RCT: FAIL -25% vs 3-RIR -8% velocity loss; 24 h residual decrement after FAIL/1-RIR) and accumulate across a block, deload/fatigue-reduction weeks back off effort to ~3-6 RIR while maintaining technique. In the trained-subject RCTs, deload weeks were programmed at reduced volume and/or held at RIR1 with halved frequency/volume (Martikainen) or reduced load (Ruple). Raising RIR is a lower-cost lever than only cutting volume because it directly removes the fatigue-generating last reps. This is a fatigue-management convention extending the acute fatigue data; direct RCT comparison of deload RIR targets is lacking.

loading_training_variables.recommended: Progress RIR DOWN within a block (e.g. start ~4 RIR, end ~1 RIR) for equal gains at lower average RPE
loading_training_variables.description: Varying proximity within a block is an EQUIVALENCE result with a fatigue advantage. Martikainen et al. 2025 (trained men/women, 10 wk): a group that ramped weekly target from RIR4 down to RIR1 across each 5-wk block matched a constant-RIR1 group on squat/bench 1RM and vastus lateralis CSA, with triceps thickness significantly increasing ONLY in the varying group, while accruing LOWER session RPE (means 6.9 vs 7.7) at equal volume-load. So an autoregulated descending-RIR scheme buys the same adaptations as grinding near failure all block, at lower perceived strain/fatigue. RIR estimation accuracy is already acceptable in trained lifters and improves with use, supporting RIR-based autoregulation.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 0-1 RIR (essentially to failure) when using light loads for hypertrophy
loading_training_variables.description: Proximity to failure becomes MORE important at low loads because high-threshold motor units are only recruited late in the set. Both Grgic 2022 and Refalo discuss Lasevicius et al.: training to failure promoted greater hypertrophy at 30% 1RM but NOT at 80% 1RM. So when loads are light (high-rep), train to or very near failure (0-1 RIR) to ensure the larger motor units/Type II fibers are stimulated; at moderate-to-heavy loads (60-85%+) recruitment is reached early and the failure requirement relaxes. This is a load-dependent qualifier on the general RIR target.

loading_training_variables.recommended: Earlier sets ~2-3 RIR, final set ~0-1 RIR (only the last set near failure)
loading_training_variables.description: A practical reconciliation: keep most working sets of a heavy compound at 2-3 RIR to preserve load and limit per-set fatigue, then take only the LAST set to 0-1 RIR to capture the closer-to-failure hypertrophy premium where it costs the least subsequent volume. Helms 2016 frames main-movement sets at RPE 6-8 (2-4 RIR) with reductions as needed on later sets; the descending within-exercise scheme limits the linear fatigue accrual Refalo documented (each near-failure set degrades the next). Equivalence/expert-derived: no RCT isolates last-set-only failure, but it follows from the dose-response (small hypertrophy slope) plus the steep fatigue cost data.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 1-5 RIR on most work sets; failure not required and may be counterproductive
loading_training_variables.description: For maximal strength the proximity-to-failure dose-response is essentially FLAT across a wide RIR range: in all of Robinson et al. 2024's best-fit strength models the marginal RIR slope CI contained the null (negligible relationship). Grgic et al. 2022 found failure vs non-failure strength ES = -0.09 (ns), and in volume-non-equated studies non-failure was actually favored (ES = -0.32, p = 0.025) because the failure groups did less total volume. Strength gains were similar across 1-5+ RIR provided volume/load are matched, so failure is not needed for strength and can even hurt it via accumulated neuromuscular fatigue degrading subsequent set quality.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 3-5 RIR on heavy compounds (most working sets), reserving 0-2 RIR for peaks/testing
loading_training_variables.description: On multi-joint barbell lifts trained for strength, stopping 3-5 reps shy of failure preserves bar speed and technique while matching the gains from harder sets. In Robinson et al. 2025 (38 trained men, 8 wk), back-squat and bench strength gains were COMPARABLE between 4-6 RIR (bench +9.05 kg, squat +13.79 kg) and 1-3 RIR (bench +9.72 kg, squat +18.05 kg), but were SLIGHTLY INFERIOR when sets reached momentary failure (0-3 RIR bench +5.07 kg; 0 RIR bench +0.71 kg), with the 0/0-3 RIR squat protocols having poor feasibility. Ruple 2023 similarly found 0-1 vs 4-6 RIR on squat/bench/deadlift produced equivalent 1RM gains over 5-6 wk. This is the key 'big fatigue cost at 0 RIR' case for big lifts.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 1-6 RIR; avoid routine 0 RIR on heavy lifts (slightly inferior + high fatigue)
loading_training_variables.description: In trained lifters, strength is preserved across a wide RIR band and routine failure tends to be counterproductive on heavy compounds. Robinson 2025 (trained men): 4-6 RIR and 1-3 RIR gave comparable bench/squat 1RM gains while 0-3 RIR and 0 RIR were slightly inferior. Ruple 2023 (trained adults): 0-1 vs 4-6 RIR gave equivalent squat/bench/deadlift 1RM gains. The Martikainen 2025 trained-subject RCT found constant RIR1 vs varying RIR1-4 produced statistically similar 1RM gains, but RIR1-4 achieved them at LOWER session RPE and with more consistent squat improvement, consistent with failure's fatigue penalty. Equivalence at matched volume is the rule; the only loss is at 0 RIR.

loading_training_variables.recommended: 1-5 RIR in accumulation; 0-1 RIR reserved for peaking/competition attempts
loading_training_variables.description: For elite/advanced strength athletes the principle holds (failure not required for strength; Robinson 2024 flat slope) but periodized peaking necessitates exposure to near-maximal, very-low-RIR efforts to express and test 1RM. The practical model from RIR-RPE programming (Helms 2016) is to autoregulate accumulation blocks at moderate RIR (1-5) and bias toward 0-1 RIR only in intensification/peak phases, since failed reps are by definition poor-quality reps that add neuromuscular fatigue disrupting subsequent sets. Evidence in true elites is sparse (most RCTs use intermediate/trained samples), so this extends the trained-lifter finding plus peaking convention.

set_structures.name: Drop set
set_structures.mechanism: Set taken to/near concentric failure, then load is immediately reduced (~10-25%) and the set continued with no rest, often repeated 2-3 times. Accumulates training volume and high metabolic stress in a short time. Volume-equated meta-analyses show EQUIVALENT growth and strength to traditional sets (Coleman ES 0.08 hypertrophy / 0.07 strength, both trivial, I2=0%; Sodal SMD 0.155 ns; Havers chronic hypertrophy SMD 0.04 ns, strength -0.04 ns). The value is TIME-EFFICIENCY — some drop-set protocols take 1/2 to 1/3 the time for equal hypertrophy — not more muscle.

set_structures.name: Rest-pause
set_structures.mechanism: A set is taken to failure, then after a short intra-set rest (~20s) the SAME load is used for further mini-sets to failure until a preplanned rep total is reached. Unlike drop sets, load is held constant — the brief rest allows phosphocreatine partial resynthesis so high loads, concentric velocity and power are maintained while accumulating volume quickly. Volume/effort-equated evidence shows similar strength and hypertrophy to traditional sets (Prestes: similar strength, ~35 vs 57 min); one study and the Tsartsapakis aggregate hint at a modest hypertrophy edge, but this is not robust volume-equated support, so framed as a TIME-EFFICIENT route to equivalent gains.

set_structures.name: Myo-reps
set_structures.mechanism: A cluster-style technique: one higher-rep 'activation' set to near-failure (RPE ~8, ~12-30 reps) primes motor-unit recruitment, then several short-rest (20-30s) 'back-off' mini-sets (3-5 reps) keep the muscle near failure to accumulate effective reps efficiently. Probably does not recruit MORE motor units than other to-failure work (rate coding accounts for the late-set output). A trained-male RCT (Liberty thesis) found COMPARABLE hypertrophy and strength to traditional protocols with reduced training duration and better recovery/stress perception — value is time-efficiency and fatigue management, not greater growth.

set_structures.name: Cluster set
set_structures.mechanism: Short intra-set rest intervals (~20-60s) are inserted between reps or small rep-blocks within a set. Exploits fast-phase phosphocreatine resynthesis to MAINTAIN bar velocity, force and power, allowing higher mechanical output / more total volume at a given (often heavy) load with LESS within-set fatigue. Chronic meta-analysis (Davies): cluster and traditional configurations are EQUALLY effective for muscular/neuromuscular adaptation, but clusters achieve them with less fatigue development. Acute meta (Jukic): clusters reduce mechanical, metabolic and perceptual fatigue. Value = fatigue management and velocity/power maintenance, not more hypertrophy.

set_structures.name: Mechanical drop set
set_structures.mechanism: Instead of reducing the load, the EXERCISE/leverage is switched to a mechanically easier variation at failure (e.g. incline-to-flat curl, stiff-bar to close-grip) to extend the set with the same weight. Like load drop sets, it accumulates extra reps and metabolic stress in a fatigued state without raising peak mechanical tension beyond the first failure point. Drop-set-family evidence (Coleman, Sodal, Havers) shows volume-equated equivalence to traditional sets, so the rationale is time-efficient volume accumulation and exhausting a muscle across strength curves, not greater hypertrophy. No mechanical-drop-set-specific trial in this corpus (extrapolated from the drop-set family).

set_structures.name: Partials / lengthened partials
set_structures.mechanism: Reps performed over a partial range of motion; the lengthened-partials variant keeps the muscle in the stretched (lengthened) portion of the ROM, where stretch-mediated tension is proposed to be a potent hypertrophy stimulus and where reps can be continued after full-ROM failure to extend a set. In this corpus partials are only referenced as a generic intensity/extended-set tool (RP guide); there is no volume-equated chronic trial here, so the supported claim is conservative — a way to extend a set and bias the lengthened position, with growth benefit over full-ROM not established by the sources read.

set_structures.name: 21s
set_structures.mechanism: A fixed partial+full-ROM set scheme: 7 reps in the lower (lengthened) half of the ROM, 7 in the upper half, then 7 full-ROM reps (21 total), extending time-under-tension and metabolic stress at a sub-maximal load. A specific, named application of the partial-rep / extended-set concept used mainly for isolation work (curls, extensions). No 21s-specific or volume-equated study exists in this corpus; under the partial-rep and advanced-technique evidence it functions as a metabolic-stress/variety finisher, with no demonstrated hypertrophy superiority over equated straight sets.

set_structures.name: Crescent / ascending pyramid
set_structures.mechanism: Load increases (and reps decrease) across successive sets within one exercise. Spans a range of loads/rep ranges in a single exercise, but when total volume is equated it produces the SAME strength, hypertrophy and muscle-architecture changes as traditional sets — Angleri (volume-equated within-subject RCT): CSA +7.5% CP vs +7.6% TRAD; leg-press 1RM +25.9% both. The Cardozo narrative review found no superior acute or chronic response. Value is variety / spanning rep ranges, NOT more growth.

set_structures.name: Reverse-pyramid training (RPT)
set_structures.mechanism: Heaviest, lowest-rep top set performed FIRST while fresh, then load is dropped on subsequent back-off sets to extend reps. The rationale is order/freshness: putting the maximal-tension set first maximises force output and neural recruitment for that set, unlike crescent pyramids where the heavy set is pre-fatigued. No direct volume-equated trial in this corpus; pyramid-family evidence (Angleri, Cardozo, Fonseca) shows pyramidal loading is equivalent to traditional for growth, so RPT's edge is theoretical strength/time efficiency, not greater hypertrophy.

set_structures.name: Straight sets (double progression)
set_structures.mechanism: Reference/control structure: fixed load and rep target across sets to failure or near-failure, with full inter-set rest. Drives hypertrophy and strength via the established primary levers (mechanical tension, volume = sets x reps, proximity to failure). Double progression = add reps within a rep range, then add load once the top of the range is hit. All advanced set structures are benchmarked against this; volume-equated meta-analyses repeatedly find no other structure superior to it for growth.

set_structures.name: Antagonist (agonist-antagonist / reciprocal) superset
set_structures.mechanism: Two exercises for OPPOSING muscle groups (e.g. bench press + bench pull, or leg extension + leg curl) performed back-to-back with little rest, then a shared rest period. Each muscle effectively rests while its antagonist works, so per-exercise performance and volume are preserved (some data show equal or higher volume than traditional order). A volume-equated 8-week RCT (SportRxiv) found the SAME muscle-thickness, strength, power, endurance and body-composition gains as traditional training while completing sessions in 36% LESS time; the Zhang meta-analysis frames supersets as a time-efficient alternative. Value is TIME-EFFICIENCY, not greater growth.

set_structures.name: Compound / agonist superset (pre-exhaustion)
set_structures.mechanism: Two exercises for the SAME muscle done back-to-back; the classic form is pre-exhaustion — a single-joint isolation move (e.g. dumbbell fly, leg extension) performed immediately before a compound (bench press, squat) to fatigue the target agonist first. Theory claims this drives greater agonist activation/hypertrophy, but EMG evidence does NOT support it: pre-exhaustion did not increase target-muscle activity in untrained (Fujita) or change pectoralis activation in trained men (Golas), and it REDUCES the reps/load achievable on the subsequent compound. So it cuts volume and offers no demonstrated growth benefit — mechanistically weak; mainly a time-efficiency/variety tool.

set_structures.name: Giant set
set_structures.mechanism: Three or more exercises performed consecutively with minimal rest, typically for one muscle group or region. An extension of the superset principle that maximises training density and local metabolic stress per unit time. Falls under the superset/advanced-density family that is time-efficient but, per the broader advanced-techniques and superset evidence (Zhang, Krzysztofik, sportsmed NMA), produces hypertrophy/strength comparable to traditional volume-matched training rather than superior growth. No giant-set-specific volume-equated trial in this corpus, so the claim is the family-level one: efficiency and metabolic stress, not more muscle.

claims.statement: Grip type, grip width, and forearm orientation on the lat pulldown meaningfully bias which region of the latissimus dorsi is trained, so a lifter can 'target' the lat differently (e.g., wide vs narrow, pronated vs supinated, neutral) to drive region-specific lat development.
claims.nuance: All three skeptic lenses refute (strength 0.90-0.95). The claim of region-specific LAT development rests entirely on acute surface-EMG proxies, and the one direct study (Brusco, 40 trained men, 7 grip variants at 70% 1RM) found NO significant difference in latissimus dorsi activation across grip type, width, or forearm orientation (LD held ~45-62% MVC regardless) and explicitly states the data 'challenge the assumption that grip targets this muscle.' What actually changes with grip is SYNERGIST loading (posterior delt, biceps, traps) and the small LD-centroid shift seen in the HD-EMG paper -- but a centroid shift is not demonstrated regional hypertrophy, and there is zero volume-equated growth data. Effect vs practical: grip choice meaningfully alters synergist recruitment, comfort, joint safety and leverage (a real reason to vary grips), but it does not steer where the lat grows. The claim conflates 'loads synergists / feels different' with 'grows different lat regions,' and even overstates equivalent activation as differential targeting.

claims.statement: Standing (knee-extended) calf raises grow the gastrocnemius more than seated (knee-flexed) calf raises, because the biarticular gastrocnemius is trained at a longer muscle length when the knee is straight; the soleus grows similarly either way.
claims.nuance: This is a genuine more-growth finding, not a false-equivalence. The growth half rests on a direct 12-week within-person MRI hypertrophy trial (Kinoshita 2023) that was both load-matched (70% 1RM) and volume/set-rep matched: standing (knee-extended) calf raises grew the gastrocnemius far more than seated (lateral +12.4% vs +1.7%, medial +9.2% vs +0.6%, d=1.53-1.58), while soleus grew similarly regardless of knee angle (+2.1% vs +2.9%, ns) -- so both halves of the claim are confirmed on a measured outcome, with the long-muscle-length mechanism corroborated by (not substituted for) the growth result. The single dissenting lens does not refute the effect direction; it flags external validity: the basis is a single uncontrolled study in n=14 untrained adults, so generalization to trained lifters is the only real weakness, and the operative variable is muscle length rather than knee position per se. Practical truth: train the gastroc with a straight knee (standing/leg-press calf raise) and the soleus with a bent knee (seated) -- the claim holds as stated, with confidence below 1.0 due to the thin, untrained evidence base.

claims.statement: The front (to-chest) lat pulldown produces greater latissimus dorsi recruitment/activation than the behind-the-neck lat pulldown, making it the superior variation for building the lats.
claims.nuance: All three lenses refute (strength 0.88-0.90). 'Superior for building the lats' rests on a single acute HD-EMG study (14 trained men, 8-RM) that is both load-confounded and phase-dependent: the front-LPD condition used ~18% greater absolute load (70.0 vs 59.3 kg) and greater bar displacement, which the authors flag as inflating front-LPD EMG, and the LD advantage appears only in the descending/concentric phase (ES 0.97) while the back-LPD LD is actually higher in the ascending/eccentric phase (ES 0.63) -- a reversal, not a clean win. Prior literature is itself mixed (Sperandei 2009 no difference; Signorile 2002 favored front). Effect vs practical: front-LPD is a defensible default because it permits heavier loading and is safer for most shoulders, and the study authors recommend programming BOTH for varied spatial stimulus -- but there is no hypertrophy data, so the growth-superiority leap is unsupported. 'Greater recruitment' is partly true (one phase, load-confounded); 'superior for building lats' is not established.

claims.statement: The incline barbell/dumbbell press preferentially biases (and preferentially grows) the clavicular/upper head of the pectoralis major relative to the flat bench press, because the inclined arm path shifts mechanical and neural emphasis to the upper pec fascicles.
claims.nuance: All three lenses flag the same fatal gap: the GROWTH half ('preferentially GROWS the clavicular head') rests on a proxy, not a direct outcome. The cited corpus contains NO flat-vs-incline trained-subject hypertrophy study -- the two provided sources (a biceps shoulder-position EMG paper and thorax anatomy texts) support only the general joint-angle-changes-activation mechanism. The biasing/ACTIVATION half is better grounded: the pectoralis major is regionally partitioned, and regional EMG (Cabral 2022, plus broader Rodriguez-Ridao 2020) shows inclining shifts excitation toward the upper/clavicular fascicles, which is why this is less wrong than the lat-grip claim. But activation predicts, it does not equal, regional hypertrophy. The one direct incline-hypertrophy data point (Chaves, single upper-site thickness, untrained) is modest and is not even cited. Effect-vs-practical: incline is a defensible tool to emphasize the upper chest, but the affirmative growth-superiority claim lacks the trained-RCT support it needs, and flat bench still trains the clavicular head substantially. Source_ids should be upgraded to a direct flat-vs-incline EMG/hypertrophy paper. Disputed: the direction is plausible and activation-supported, but the growth claim rests on mechanism/proxy and out-of-corpus work.

claims.statement: The barbell hip thrust produces greater gluteus maximus activation than the back squat and is therefore the superior exercise for growing the glutes.
claims.nuance: All three lenses converge on a textbook EMG-to-growth leap. The activation premise is true: the barbell hip thrust elicits higher gluteus maximus surface EMG than the back squat (Contreras 2015, n=13 trained women, ~10RM: mean upper GMax 69.5% vs 29.4%; Neto 2020 review ~75% vs ~53% MVIC). But the 'therefore superior for growing the glutes' conclusion does not follow: (1) acute surface EMG does not reliably predict chronic hypertrophy -- Contreras 2015 itself calls for longitudinal studies and Neto flags EMG misinterpretation; (2) the corpus has NO volume-/effort-equated hypertrophy trial showing the hip thrust grows glutes more, and matched-volume RCTs in the broader literature show similar growth with region-specific biases; (3) the hip thrust is not even the highest-EMG glute exercise (step-ups exceed both). Practical truth: the hip thrust is an excellent, possibly preferable glute exercise for practical reasons (high tension at short muscle lengths, low spinal/systemic fatigue, easy to load and progress), but it is not established as superior for glute hypertrophy. The growth-superiority conclusion is refuted; the activation premise stands.

claims.statement: The rectus femoris is hard to target/develop because, as a biarticular muscle, it suffers active insufficiency: it cannot be fully activated for knee extension when the hip is flexed (e.g., seated leg extension), so much of the muscle (especially the distal region) is never strongly recruited in common quad exercises.
claims.nuance: The claim mixes a real phenomenon with a load-bearing mechanistic detail that the cited literature contradicts. SUPPORTED: the rectus femoris is biarticular and does exhibit active insufficiency in the length-tension sense -- it is a weaker knee extensor when the hip is flexed/shortened (StatPearls), and Miyamoto 2012 confirms task-dependent, regional control. REFUTED (the falsifiable core): the assertion that 'the distal region is never strongly recruited in common quad exercises' is backwards. Miyamoto plus direct knee-extension training studies (Narici, Blazevich) show the distal/middle RF preferentially contributes to KNEE EXTENSION and grows MORE distally from knee-extension training -- so in seated leg extension the distal RF is exactly the region that IS strongly driven; it is the PROXIMAL region biased to hip flexion that under-activates. Lenses split on framing: the volume-equation lens correctly notes this is a negative trainability/mechanism claim rather than a superiority claim (so that lens doesn't bite), while the anatomy-focused lenses refute the backwards distal-recruitment detail. The grain of truth: because RF crosses the hip, its overall knee-extension contribution is partly blunted when the hip is flexed, favoring less-hip-flexed positions for fuller stimulus. Practical takeaway (train RF in more hip-extended positions; it may lag with hip-flexed-only work) is defensible; the stated mechanism is not. Disputed.

claims.statement: The hip thrust biases the glutes toward their shortened/peak-contracted length while the squat (and deep hip hinges) load the glutes at a long/stretched length, so the two are complementary rather than redundant for complete glute development.
claims.nuance: The short-length (hip thrust, peak contraction at full hip extension) vs long-length (squat/RDL, glute stretched at deep hip flexion) contrast is anatomically real and a sound programming rationale for complementary coverage. But the claimed payoff (combining the two yields MORE/complete glute development than doing more of either alone) is mechanism plus borrowed within-person length studies, with no head-to-head trial demonstrating an additive growth benefit. One lens accepts it as a complementarity principle (the lean itself declines to claim a quantified additive growth advantage); two lenses flag it as proxy/leverage reasoning. Honest finding: defensible as a complementary-coverage heuristic, NOT as a proven extra-growth claim. This is the constructive flip-side of the refuted 'hip thrust grows glutes more' claim: the hip thrust's value is the short-length emphasis it adds, not superior total growth.

claims.statement: Increasing the stretch/ROM of a hip hinge — e.g., a deficit or step Romanian deadlift, or pulling to a deeper stretch — increases posterior-chain stimulus and hamstring/glute growth versus a shorter-ROM version.
claims.nuance: All three lenses refute, though they agree the longer-length DIRECTION is plausible. The step/deficit-RDL-specific evidence is acute EMG (Coratella: step-RDL increased excitation of GMax, semitendinosus, and erector spinae vs standard and stiff-leg RDL) — activation, not growth. The growth-level backing is BORROWED from a different movement: Maeo's lengthened-partial hip-extension MRI study (training the 90-45 deg lengthened range grew hip extensors ~2x more than full ROM), in untrained subjects. No trained-subject RCT directly tests deficit/step RDL vs standard RDL for hamstring/glute hypertrophy, so the named comparison's advantage is extrapolated from the general longer-length principle plus exercise-specific EMG, not directly measured. Honest finding: the longer-ROM-grows-more direction is corroborated by hypertrophy trials on OTHER movements, so it is a well-reasoned heuristic, but the specific step/deficit-RDL superiority is proxy + extrapolation. Practical cap: erector-spinae fatigue limits usable extra hinge ROM.

claims.statement: A supinated (underhand) pulldown grip shifts work to the biceps while a pronated grip preferentially trains the lats/back.
claims.nuance: The folk rule fails on its own terms: Sperandei found biceps AND latissimus activation statistically the SAME across pronated and supinated pulldown grips, so the 'underhand = arms, overhand = back' split has neither EMG nor any volume-equated growth support. Two lenses refute it; the third (refuted=false) agrees, noting this negative claim survives the lens precisely because the only proxy behind the popular rule found no difference.
